description: Bounds of the drop cap candidate signal and of the pass that acts on a verdict. A drop cap is an oversized initial standing at the head of a piece of running text, and it is found here from three general typographic facts and no publication specific one. 'min_first_run_size_ratio' is how large the paragraph's opening character run must be against that paragraph's own median character size: an initial set three lines tall is several times the body size, while a paragraph opening in small caps or bold is barely above it. 'max_first_run_chars' is how many non-space characters that run may carry, which is what separates an initial from a heading or a lead-in phrase that happens to be set larger. 'initial_size_tolerance' is how far two character sizes may differ and still count as one run, in points; it is the tolerance the styling stage merges two styles under, so the run this reads is the run that stage would have grouped. The run is read from the paragraph's leading characters rather than from its first composition, because the composition holding an initial is not always a style run: where the styling stage reads the body sized letters after an enlarged initial as corner marks, the initial and the rest of the first word arrive inside one formula, and a reader that consults the first style run alone finds nothing there at all. 'max_body_rank_in_article' is how far into its article the paragraph may stand, counted over the body text paragraphs of that article in page order; a paragraph on the page its article opens on qualifies whatever its rank, because that is where a piece's opening initial goes. The three corpus drop caps stand at ranks 3, 5 and 5, so the bound is set at the deepest of them and holds each of them without relying on the opening page rule. 'excerpt_chars' bounds the opening of the paragraph quoted into the review draft, which is what a human reads to recognise the paragraph; it steers no decision. 'separator_policy' governs the one character the merge has to decide about. A paragraph finder that assembles an initial and the word it opens into one paragraph puts a space between them where the drawing positions leave a gap, and that space is synthesised: it carries no xobject id because no content stream drew it. Under 'drop_synthesized' such a space is removed when the runs are merged, which is what turns a first word split in two back into one word; a space the source itself drew is always kept, so an initial that stands as a word of its own keeps its space. Under 'keep' nothing is removed and the merge only changes what carries the characters. The limit of the rule is that a source drawing no space at all after a one letter word leaves the two cases indistinguishable at this layer, so every join is recorded in the sidecar with the text before and after it. 'decision_sources' is the closed set of answers to where the verdict a paragraph was acted on under came from, and 'apply_fields' is the shape of one such record, both asserted against what the pass builds so the report's format is declared here rather than implied by the code. 'default_decision_by_target' is what a candidate nobody ruled is acted on under, one entry per target language, matched to a run by the longest declared prefix of its target language tag; a target language no entry claims leaves every unruled candidate alone. Chinese declares 'flatten' because Chinese typesetting has no drop cap convention and a Latin initial left standing in a Chinese paragraph is the defect this answers; English declares 'keep' because there the initial is the design. Every value is checked against the verdict vocabulary declared in configs/hitl.json, which is the one place a verdict is named.

default_decision_by_target.description: One verdict per target language, keyed by language tag. A run's target language selects the entry whose key is the longest prefix of it, as the standing translation instruction selects its role text. Only a marked candidate is decided this way: a paragraph the marking pass did not find is left alone whatever this says, because the machine default is an answer to a finding and not a sweep.
